description: Design a message starting from the audience's existing beliefs, vocabulary, and concerns, then bridge to your point. Works for sales pitches, personal conversations, policy memos, or any message where landing matters more than sending.

steps.description: Map what the audience already believes about the topic before you say anything. List their assumptions, prior experiences, and emotional associations. If you skip this step, you are guessing at a frame instead of building on one.

inputs.name: topic-or-proposal
inputs.desc: The thing you need to communicate

inputs.name: audience-description
inputs.desc: Who you are communicating to (role, relationship, context)

outputs.name: belief-map
outputs.desc: List of the audience's existing beliefs, assumptions, and emotional associations about this topic

outputs.name: knowledge-gaps
outputs.desc: What the audience does not know or has wrong that matters for your message

process: Write down everything the audience likely believes about this topic based on their role, past interactions, and context.
For each belief, note whether it helps your message (an anchor you can build on) or hurts it (a frame you need to reframe).
Identify knowledge gaps: things they do not know that would change their position if they did.
Flag emotional associations. A CFO hearing 'new platform' feels risk. A designer hearing 'standardize' feels constraint. Name the feeling, not just the fact.

steps.description: Identify the exact words and phrases the audience uses to describe the problem, the domain, and what success looks like. Your message must use their words, not yours.

inputs.name: belief-map
inputs.desc: The audience's existing beliefs and assumptions

outputs.name: vocabulary-list
outputs.desc: The specific words and phrases the audience uses for this topic, with notes on connotation

outputs.name: words-to-avoid
outputs.desc: Words that trigger resistance, confusion, or the wrong frame in this audience

process: List the words the audience actually uses when they talk about this problem. Pull from emails, meetings, Slack messages, or past conversations.
Note connotations: 'investment' vs. 'cost' vs. 'spend' are the same dollar amount with different emotional weight.
Identify jargon that signals in-group membership. Using the right jargon builds trust. Using the wrong jargon signals outsider.
List words to avoid: terms that trigger automatic resistance, carry baggage from past failures, or map to a frame you do not want.

steps.description: Define what the audience wants to be true after receiving your message. Their desired outcome is not your desired outcome. Your message succeeds when it connects the two.

inputs.name: vocabulary-list
inputs.desc: How the audience talks about this topic

outputs.name: audience-desired-outcome
outputs.desc: What the audience wants to happen, in their own framing

outputs.name: your-desired-outcome
outputs.desc: What you want to happen

outputs.name: overlap-zone
outputs.desc: Where the two outcomes align, which becomes the foundation of your message

process: State what the audience wants from this interaction. Not what you think they should want. What they actually want.
State what you want from this interaction. Be honest. If you want approval, say approval. If you want behavior change, say behavior change.
Find the overlap: the place where giving them what they want also moves you toward what you want. This is your message's center of gravity.
If there is no overlap, your message cannot work as designed. Either change what you are asking for, or change who you are asking.

steps.description: Write the bridge sentence: the single sentence that connects the audience's current frame to your message. The bridge uses their vocabulary, acknowledges their concern, and introduces your point as a natural extension of what they already want.

outputs.name: bridge-sentence
outputs.desc: The single sentence that connects their frame to your message

outputs.name: supporting-points
outputs.desc: 2-3 points that reinforce the bridge, each using the audience's vocabulary

process: Draft the bridge sentence using this structure: '[What they want] + [your mechanism for getting there].' Example: 'You want predictable costs (their want), and this contract structure caps your exposure at $X (your mechanism).'
Test the bridge: does it use their words? Does it start from their concern? Does it feel like agreement rather than argument?
Write 2-3 supporting points, each reinforcing the bridge. Each point should use their vocabulary and reference their desired outcome.
Cut any point that requires the audience to adopt your frame before they can understand it. Those go later, not here.

steps.description: Arrange the full message in the order the audience can receive it: bridge first, then supporting evidence, then the ask. Most messages fail because they put the ask before the bridge.

inputs.name: bridge-sentence
inputs.desc: The sentence connecting their frame to yours

inputs.name: knowledge-gaps
inputs.desc: What they need to learn for the message to work

outputs.name: message-sequence
outputs.desc: The full message in delivery order: bridge, evidence, gap-fill, ask

outputs.name: delivery-notes
outputs.desc: Notes on tone, medium, and timing for delivery

process: Open with the bridge sentence. This is the first thing the audience hears or reads.
Follow with the supporting points, ordered by what matters most to them (not to you).
Fill knowledge gaps only where needed to support the ask. Do not educate for its own sake.
Place the ask last. By this point, the ask should feel like the logical conclusion of everything before it.
Add delivery notes: what medium suits this message (email, in-person, phone), what tone, and when to send it (timing relative to the audience's decision cycle).

steps.description: Test the message against the most likely resistance points. For each point of resistance, check whether the message already addresses it. If not, revise before sending.

inputs.name: message-sequence
inputs.desc: The full message in delivery order

inputs.name: belief-map
inputs.desc: The audience's existing beliefs, including ones that conflict with your message

outputs.name: resistance-points
outputs.desc: The top 3-5 points where the audience will push back, with the real concern underneath each

outputs.name: revised-message
outputs.desc: The message after incorporating pre-emptive responses to the top resistance points

process: Read the message as the audience would. At each sentence, ask: where would they stop agreeing?
For each resistance point, name the stated objection and the real concern underneath it. 'Too expensive' usually means 'I am not sure of the return.'
Check whether the message already addresses the real concern. If yes, verify the address is in the audience's vocabulary.
If not addressed, insert a pre-emptive sentence that acknowledges the concern and provides evidence. Pre-emption is stronger than rebuttal.
Cut any pre-emption that makes the message longer than the audience's attention span. Prioritize the top 3 concerns.

description: Map every possible objection to any proposal, plan, or ask. For each objection, find the stated concern, the real concern underneath it, and the honest response. Group by underlying concern and pre-empt the top three in your initial message. Works for sales, negotiations, internal proposals, and personal requests.

steps.description: List every element of your proposal that touches someone's budget, authority, status, workload, or comfort. These are the surfaces where objections grow.

inputs.name: proposal-description
inputs.desc: The proposal, plan, or ask you need to defend

inputs.name: stakeholder-list
inputs.desc: Who will be affected by or must approve this proposal

outputs.name: objection-surfaces
outputs.desc: List of proposal elements that touch budget, authority, status, workload, or comfort for each stakeholder

outputs.name: stakeholder-exposure-map
outputs.desc: For each stakeholder, what this proposal costs them (money, time, power, convenience)

process: For each element of the proposal, ask: who pays for this, who loses authority, who has more work, who looks bad, who is uncomfortable?
Map each stakeholder to the specific cost they bear. A proposal with zero cost to a stakeholder gets zero objection from that stakeholder.
Rank stakeholders by how much the proposal costs them. The person who loses the most will object the loudest.
Note asymmetries: if the proposal benefits person A at the expense of person B, person B's objection is predictable and rational.

steps.description: Collect every stated objection you have heard or can predict. Stated objections are what people say out loud. They are almost never the real concern.

outputs.name: stated-objections
outputs.desc: List of every stated objection, attributed to the stakeholder likely to raise it

outputs.name: frequency-ranking
outputs.desc: Objections ranked by how often they are raised (past data or prediction)

process: List every objection you have heard in previous conversations, meetings, or emails about this or similar proposals.
For each stakeholder, predict what they will say based on their exposure map. Use their actual vocabulary.
Rank by frequency: the objection raised by the most stakeholders, or raised most often, goes first.
Include the objections that are whispered but never said in meetings. Those are often the real blockers.

steps.description: For each stated objection, find the real concern underneath it. 'Too expensive' means 'I do not trust the return.' 'Not the right time' means 'I do not want to own the risk.' The stated objection is the symptom. The real concern is the diagnosis.

inputs.name: stated-objections
inputs.desc: What people say when they object

outputs.name: concern-pairs
outputs.desc: For each stated objection: the stated version, the real concern, and the evidence for why the real concern is what it is

outputs.name: concern-clusters
outputs.desc: Objections grouped by their shared real concern

process: For each stated objection, apply the 'what would change their mind' test: if I addressed this objection perfectly, would they agree? If not, the stated objection is not the real concern.
Map the stated objection to the stakeholder's exposure. The real concern almost always maps to the biggest thing they lose.
Group objections that share the same underlying concern. Five different stated objections from one stakeholder often trace to one real concern.
Write the real concern in plain language. No jargon, no softening. 'They are afraid they will be blamed if this fails' is a real concern.

steps.description: Write the honest response to each real concern. An honest response acknowledges the concern, provides evidence, and does not pretend the cost is zero. If the concern is valid, say so and explain how you mitigate it.

inputs.name: concern-pairs
inputs.desc: Stated objection paired with real concern

inputs.name: proposal-description
inputs.desc: The proposal, so responses stay grounded in what is actually being proposed

outputs.name: response-map
outputs.desc: For each real concern: the honest response, the evidence supporting it, and the residual risk if any

outputs.name: unresolvable-concerns
outputs.desc: Concerns that cannot be addressed honestly, which become negotiation points or deal-breakers

process: For each real concern, write a response that starts with acknowledgment: 'You are right that this adds workload to your team.'
Follow with evidence: data, precedent, or a structural mitigation (not a promise). 'The pilot showed 12 hours per week, and we staff a dedicated resource for the first 90 days.'
Name the residual risk honestly. 'There is still a chance the migration takes longer than estimated. Here is the fallback plan.'
If a concern cannot be resolved, flag it as a negotiation point. Do not pretend it is resolved when it is not.

steps.description: Take the top three concerns by frequency and build them into your initial message so the audience does not have to raise them. Pre-emption is stronger than rebuttal because it shows you thought about their position before they had to defend it.

inputs.name: frequency-ranking
inputs.desc: Which objections come up most often

inputs.name: concern-clusters
inputs.desc: Groups of objections sharing the same root concern

outputs.name: pre-emption-statements
outputs.desc: 3 statements to include in the initial message, each addressing a top concern before it is raised

outputs.name: remaining-response-playbook
outputs.desc: Responses for the concerns not pre-empted, ready to use when they come up in discussion

process: Select the top 3 concern clusters by frequency. These are the objections most people will have.
For each, write a pre-emption statement that acknowledges the concern and provides the evidence in 1-2 sentences.
Place the pre-emption statements after your bridge and before your ask. They should feel like 'I already thought about this' not 'I am defending myself.'
For all remaining concerns, organize responses into a playbook. Each entry: trigger phrase (what they will say), real concern, response, evidence.

steps.description: Test the objection map against a hostile audience. Have someone argue against the proposal using only the map's stated objections. If a new objection surfaces, the map has a gap. If a response fails to land, the response needs revision.

inputs.name: pre-emption-statements
inputs.desc: The statements built into the initial message

outputs.name: stress-test-results
outputs.desc: Which responses held, which failed, and which new objections surfaced

outputs.name: final-objection-map
outputs.desc: The revised and tested objection map, ready for live use

process: Run through the proposal with a skeptical colleague or role-play the objections yourself. Use the stated objections verbatim.
For each response, check: did it address the real concern? Did it use evidence? Did it feel honest or defensive?
Note any new objections that were not on the map. Add them with their real concern and response.
Revise any response that felt defensive, dismissive, or unsupported. The final map should feel like preparation, not argumentation.

description: Structure for delivering hard news or raising uncomfortable topics. Uses the Observation-Impact-Request-Silence framework. Works for firing someone, ending a relationship, raising a performance issue, or delivering bad news to a client. The silence at the end is where the real conversation happens.

steps.description: Assess what is at stake for both sides before the conversation. If you do not know what the other person stands to lose, you cannot deliver the message in a way they can receive.

inputs.name: situation-description
inputs.desc: What happened and what needs to be addressed

inputs.name: relationship-context
inputs.desc: Your relationship to the other person (boss, partner, client, friend, direct report)

outputs.name: your-stakes
outputs.desc: What you stand to lose or gain from this conversation

outputs.name: their-stakes
outputs.desc: What the other person stands to lose or gain

outputs.name: conversation-goal
outputs.desc: The specific outcome you need from this conversation, stated in one sentence

process: Write down what you stand to lose if this conversation goes badly (the relationship, a project, credibility, peace of mind).
Write down what the other person stands to lose (their job, their self-image, a project they own, the relationship with you).
State the conversation goal in one sentence. 'I need X to change by Y date' or 'I need to communicate Z and preserve the working relationship.'
If you cannot state the goal in one sentence, you are not ready for the conversation.

steps.description: Write the observation: the specific, factual, non-interpretive description of what happened. No adjectives, no intent attribution, no generalizations. 'You were late to three meetings this week' not 'You do not respect people's time.'

inputs.name: conversation-goal
inputs.desc: What you need from this conversation

outputs.name: observation-statement
outputs.desc: The factual, non-interpretive description of what happened

outputs.name: removed-interpretations
outputs.desc: Interpretations and judgments you removed from the observation

process: Write what happened using only observable facts: dates, times, specific actions, specific words said. No 'always' or 'never.'
Remove every adjective that is an interpretation. 'Late' is observable. 'Disrespectful' is an interpretation.
Remove every attribution of intent. You do not know why they did it. You know what they did.
Test: could a security camera or a transcript confirm every word in your observation? If not, it contains interpretation.

steps.description: Write the impact: what the observation caused. Impact is on you, the team, the relationship, or the outcome. Impact is felt, not judged. 'When you missed the deadline, the client escalated to the VP' not 'You are unreliable.'

inputs.name: observation-statement
inputs.desc: The factual description of what happened

inputs.name: their-stakes
inputs.desc: What the other person stands to lose, so the impact statement addresses what they care about

outputs.name: impact-statement
outputs.desc: The specific consequences of the observed behavior, stated without judgment

outputs.name: emotional-impact-note
outputs.desc: How the situation made you feel, stated as 'I felt X' not 'You made me feel X'

process: State the concrete consequences: what happened as a result of the behavior. Lost money, lost time, damaged relationship, missed opportunity.
State the emotional impact using 'I' language: 'I felt unsupported' not 'You were unsupportive.'
Connect the impact to something the other person cares about, using their stakes. If they care about the client, lead with the client impact.
Keep the impact statement to 2-3 sentences. Longer impact statements feel like an attack, not information.

steps.description: Write the request: the specific behavior change or decision you need. A request without specifics is a complaint. 'I need you to submit the draft by Wednesday at 5pm' not 'I need you to be more responsible.'

inputs.name: conversation-goal
inputs.desc: What you need from this conversation

outputs.name: request-statement
outputs.desc: The specific, actionable request

outputs.name: measurable-check
outputs.desc: How both parties will know whether the request has been met

process: State the specific behavior change or decision you need. Use a verb, a deadline, and a deliverable.
Make the request about behavior, not character. You can change behavior. You cannot change character in a conversation.
Define how both of you will know whether the request has been met. If you cannot measure it, the request is too vague.
Keep the request to one sentence. Multiple requests dilute each other.

steps.description: After Observation, Impact, and Request: stop talking. The silence is where the other person processes and responds. Most people fill the silence with softening, backtracking, or over-explaining, and the message is lost.

inputs.name: their-stakes
inputs.desc: What the other person stands to lose, which predicts their likely response

outputs.name: silence-plan
outputs.desc: What you will do during the silence (count to 10, breathe, wait) and what you will NOT do (soften, restate, apologize for asking)

outputs.name: response-paths
outputs.desc: The 3-4 likely responses and how to handle each: agreement, deflection, anger, counter-attack

process: Plan the silence: after delivering the request, count to 10 internally. Do not speak. The discomfort is the conversation working.

Map the likely responses: agreement (accept and schedule follow-up), deflection (redirect to the observation), anger (acknowledge the emotion without withdrawing the request), counter-attack (stay on the observation, do not argue about intent).
For each response path, write one sentence you will say. Keep it short. Long responses after silence undo the silence.
Plan the close: restate the request, confirm the measurable check, and set the follow-up date.

steps.description: Rehearse the full conversation: observation, impact, request, silence. Say it out loud. Hearing your own words reveals where you slip from observation into interpretation, from impact into accusation, and from request into venting.

outputs.name: rehearsal-notes
outputs.desc: Where you stumbled, softened, or slipped into interpretation during rehearsal

outputs.name: final-conversation-script
outputs.desc: The revised, rehearsed conversation script ready for delivery

process: Say the observation, impact, and request out loud, in order. Record yourself if possible.
Listen for interpretation creeping in: 'you always,' 'you never,' 'I think you meant to,' 'it seems like you.'
Listen for softening: 'I might be wrong, but,' 'this is just my perception,' 'I do not want to make a big deal of this.' These phrases give the other person permission to dismiss the message.
Revise and repeat until you can deliver all three parts in under 60 seconds without interpretation, softening, or judgment.

description: Present data as a story using the Situation-Complication-Resolution framework. One chart per point. The chart title is the conclusion, not the axis label. Everything else goes in the appendix. Works for board presentations, investor updates, team meetings, and any context where data must produce a decision.

steps.description: Define the decision the data must support. If the data is not aimed at a decision, it is decoration. Start with: what will the audience do differently after seeing this data?

inputs.name: dataset-description
inputs.desc: What data you have and what it covers

inputs.name: audience-and-decision
inputs.desc: Who will see this data and what decision they need to make

outputs.name: decision-statement
outputs.desc: The specific decision this data must inform, stated in one sentence

outputs.name: data-relevance-filter
outputs.desc: Which parts of the dataset matter for this decision and which are noise

process: Write the decision in one sentence: 'Should we expand into market X?' or 'Should we continue funding project Y?'
For each data element, ask: does this change the decision? If removing it would not change what the audience decides, cut it.
Note what data is missing that would change the decision. Missing data is more important than present data.
If the data does not point toward a decision, say so. Presenting inconclusive data as conclusive is worse than presenting nothing.

steps.description: Write the Situation: the context the audience already knows. This grounds the story in shared reality. If the audience does not recognize the situation, your complication will not register.

outputs.name: situation-statement
outputs.desc: 1-3 sentences establishing the context the audience already agrees on

outputs.name: shared-assumptions
outputs.desc: The assumptions embedded in the situation that the audience accepts without evidence

process: Write the situation in the audience's own language. 'We launched product X in Q1 targeting mid-market buyers.'
Include only facts the audience already accepts. The situation is not where you argue. It is where you establish common ground.
Test: would every person in the audience nod at every sentence? If anyone would push back, move that sentence to the complication.

steps.description: Select the single data point or finding that disrupts the situation. The complication is the reason this data matters. Without a complication, data is a status report, not a story.

inputs.name: data-relevance-filter
inputs.desc: Which data matters for the decision

outputs.name: complication-finding
outputs.desc: The single data point that disrupts the status quo

outputs.name: complication-chart
outputs.desc: Specification for the one chart that shows the complication, with title as the conclusion

process: Find the data point that breaks the audience's expectation. The complication is the gap between what they expected and what the data shows.
If multiple data points complicate the story, pick the one with the largest gap from expectation. One complication per story.
Specify the chart: the title is the conclusion ('Retention dropped 22% after pricing change'), not a description ('Q3 Retention Rates').
Annotate the chart to guide the eye: highlight the data point, add a reference line for the expectation, label the gap.

steps.description: Write the Resolution: what the data means for the decision. The resolution is not 'here is more data.' The resolution is 'therefore, we should do X.'

inputs.name: decision-statement
inputs.desc: The decision this data must inform

outputs.name: resolution-statement
outputs.desc: 1-2 sentences stating what the data means for the decision and what action it supports

outputs.name: confidence-level
outputs.desc: How confident you are in the recommendation, with what would increase or decrease confidence

process: Write the resolution as: 'Given [complication], we should [action] because [reason].'
State your confidence level honestly. 'High confidence: three quarters of data show the same trend.' Or 'Moderate confidence: one quarter of data, but the signal is strong.'
Name what would change the recommendation. 'If Q4 shows recovery, we should revisit.' This builds credibility.
Do not hedge the recommendation with 'perhaps' or 'we might consider.' State it. The audience can disagree.

steps.description: Everything that does not serve the Situation-Complication-Resolution goes in the appendix. The appendix is for people who want to check your work, not for people who need to make the decision.

inputs.name: data-relevance-filter
inputs.desc: What matters vs. what is noise

outputs.name: appendix-contents
outputs.desc: List of supporting data, methodology, and additional charts for the appendix

outputs.name: main-presentation-contents
outputs.desc: Only: situation, complication chart, resolution. Nothing else in the main body.

process: Move every chart except the complication chart to the appendix.
Move methodology, sample sizes, caveats, and alternative analyses to the appendix.
The main presentation should fit on 3 slides or one page: situation (1), complication with chart (1), resolution (1).
Test: if the audience reads only the main body, do they have enough to make the decision? If yes, the appendix is correctly separated.

steps.description: Present the story (situation, complication, resolution) to a test audience of one. Time it. If it takes longer than 3 minutes to tell the story before questions, it is too long.

outputs.name: dry-run-notes
outputs.desc: Where the story lost attention, felt unclear, or provoked the wrong questions

outputs.name: final-narrative-package
outputs.desc: The revised story, chart, and appendix ready for the real audience

process: Tell the story to one person who knows nothing about the data. Situation, complication, resolution. Time it.
If they ask a question during the story, the story is missing something. If they ask a question after, the story worked.
If any question is answered by the appendix, good. If any question is not answered by the appendix, add it.
The final package: main story (under 3 minutes), one chart, appendix for reference. Nothing else.

description: Design escalation paths for any organization or system. Define triggers, receivers, authority levels, and response times. Build in skip-level paths for emergencies. Test with a drill. An untested escalation path is a wish, not a plan.

steps.description: Define what triggers an escalation. Be specific: not 'when things go wrong' but 'when a customer-facing system is down for more than 15 minutes' or 'when a complaint mentions legal action.'

inputs.name: system-or-org-description
inputs.desc: The system, team, or organization the escalation path serves

inputs.name: historical-incidents
inputs.desc: Past incidents that should have triggered escalation (whether or not they did)

outputs.name: trigger-catalog
outputs.desc: List of specific, measurable escalation triggers with thresholds

outputs.name: severity-levels
outputs.desc: Severity tiers (typically 3-5) with clear criteria for each

process: List every incident from the past year that required someone above the front line to get involved. These are your historical triggers.
For each incident, define the measurable condition that should have triggered escalation: a time threshold, a count threshold, a keyword, or a severity rating.

Group triggers into severity levels. Level 1 is business-threatening (data breach, system-wide outage, safety incident). Level 3 is important but not urgent (delayed shipment, moderate customer complaint).
For each severity level, define the response time: Level 1 within 15 minutes, Level 2 within 1 hour, Level 3 within 4 hours. These are targets, not promises.

steps.description: Map who receives each escalation level. The receiver must have the authority to act on the escalation. A receiver without authority is a relay, not a resolution.

outputs.name: receiver-map
outputs.desc: For each severity level: primary receiver, backup receiver, and what authority they have to act

outputs.name: authority-gaps
outputs.desc: Places where the receiver does not have authority to resolve the issue and needs to escalate further

process: For each severity level, name the specific person (not a role, a person) who receives the escalation during business hours and after hours.
For each receiver, state their authority: can they spend money, reassign people, shut down a system, communicate to customers, or only relay upward?
Name the backup for each receiver. If the primary is unavailable, the backup must have the same authority.
Identify authority gaps: where does the receiver need to escalate further to get resolution? These gaps add delay. Minimize them for Level 1.

steps.description: Build a skip-level escalation path for genuine emergencies that bypasses the normal chain. When the building is on fire, you do not file a ticket.

outputs.name: skip-level-criteria
outputs.desc: Specific conditions under which the normal path is bypassed

outputs.name: skip-level-path
outputs.desc: Who to contact directly and how, with alternate contact methods

process: Define the criteria for skip-level: multiple systems down, safety risk, legal or regulatory deadline within hours, revenue impact above a threshold.
Name the person who receives skip-level escalations. This is usually the executive on call or the incident commander.
Provide at least 3 contact methods: phone (not voicemail), text, and a secondary channel (Slack DM, Teams, personal email).
Make the criteria unambiguous so the person escalating does not have to make a judgment call under pressure.

steps.description: Write templates for escalation messages at each severity level. Templates reduce the time to escalate and ensure the receiver gets the information they need to act.

outputs.name: template-set
outputs.desc: Message templates for each severity level: what happened, what is affected, what has been tried, what is needed

outputs.name: information-checklist
outputs.desc: The minimum information required for each severity level before escalating

process: For each severity level, write a template with these fields: what happened (one sentence), what is affected (systems, customers, revenue), what has been tried, what is needed from the receiver.
Keep templates to 5 lines maximum. The receiver should be able to read it in 30 seconds.
Include an information checklist: the minimum facts needed before escalating. For Level 1, the checklist is short (what and how bad). For Level 3, it is longer (what, why, what you tried).
Template language should be neutral and factual. No apologies, no blame, no speculation about cause. Facts only.

steps.description: Test the escalation path with a drill. An untested escalation path fails at the worst possible moment because someone's phone number changed, someone's authority was revoked, or someone assumed someone else would act.

inputs.name: template-set
inputs.desc: The templates to use during the drill

outputs.name: drill-results
outputs.desc: What worked, what failed, response times measured against targets

outputs.name: path-revisions
outputs.desc: Specific changes to the escalation path based on drill findings

process: Schedule the drill. Warn participants that a drill will happen this week but not when. (Fully unannounced drills test the path. Pre-announced drills test nothing.)
Trigger a simulated Level 2 escalation using the template. Measure: time to first response, time to correct receiver, time to resolution action.
Test the skip-level path separately with a simulated Level 1. Measure: did the skip-level contact respond within 15 minutes?
After the drill, compare actual response times to targets. Every gap is a revision. Update contact info, authority grants, and templates.

steps.description: Set up ongoing maintenance for the escalation path. Contact info changes, people leave, authority shifts. An escalation path that is not maintained decays within months.

outputs.name: maintenance-schedule
outputs.desc: When and how the escalation path is reviewed and updated

outputs.name: final-escalation-path-document
outputs.desc: The complete, tested, and maintained escalation path

process: Set a quarterly review: verify all contact info, confirm all receivers still have the required authority, and update the org chart mapping.
Set a semi-annual drill: run a Level 2 drill every 6 months. Run a Level 1 skip-level drill annually.
Assign an owner for the escalation path document. If no one owns it, no one maintains it.
Store the document where it can be accessed during an outage. If the document lives in a system that can go down, print a copy.

description: Build a status update system people actually read. Match update frequency to the audience's decision frequency. Include only what changed, what is blocked, and what the outlook is. Remove everything the audience can look up themselves. Shorter is read. Longer is filed.

steps.description: Map each audience segment to their decision frequency. Daily updates for a weekly decision-maker is noise. Weekly updates for a daily decision-maker is too slow. Match the cadence to when decisions happen.

inputs.name: project-or-system-description
inputs.desc: What the status updates will cover

inputs.name: stakeholder-groups
inputs.desc: The groups who need updates and what decisions they make based on them

outputs.name: audience-decision-map
outputs.desc: For each stakeholder group: their decisions, decision frequency, and therefore their ideal update cadence

outputs.name: update-schedule
outputs.desc: The update schedule: who gets what, when

process: For each stakeholder group, name the decisions they make that depend on this information. If they make no decisions from it, they do not need the update.
Match update frequency to decision frequency: if they decide weekly, update weekly (the day before their decision meeting). If they decide daily, update daily.
Eliminate audiences who consume updates out of habit, not decision-making. Politely remove them from the distribution and offer opt-in.
Publish the schedule so everyone knows when to expect updates and stops asking for ad-hoc reports.

steps.description: For each audience, include only the information they need to make their decision. Remove everything they can look up themselves. The goal is the shortest update that supports the decision, not the most complete update.

inputs.name: audience-decision-map
inputs.desc: What each group decides and when

inputs.name: project-or-system-description
inputs.desc: The full set of available information

outputs.name: content-spec-per-audience
outputs.desc: For each audience: what to include (delta, blockers, outlook) and what to exclude (available elsewhere, not decision-relevant)

outputs.name: self-service-pointer
outputs.desc: For excluded information, where the audience can find it themselves if they want it

process: For each audience, list every piece of information they currently receive in updates.
For each piece, ask: does this change their decision? If no, cut it.
For each piece, ask: can they get this from a dashboard, document, or tool themselves? If yes, cut it and point them there.
What remains: delta (what changed since last update), blockers (what is stuck and what is needed to unstick it), and outlook (is the trajectory on track, slipping, or improving).

steps.description: Design a consistent format so readers can scan the update in under 60 seconds. The format never changes. When the format changes, readers have to re-learn how to read it, and they stop reading.

outputs.name: update-template
outputs.desc: The standard format: header, delta section, blockers section, outlook section, with character limits

outputs.name: format-rules
outputs.desc: Rules that keep the format consistent across writers and over time

process: Design the template: header (project name, date, one-line summary), delta (bulleted list of what changed), blockers (each with owner and needed action), outlook (on track, at risk, or off track with one sentence why).
Set character limits: total update under 300 words. Delta under 150 words. Each blocker in one sentence. Outlook in one sentence.
Write format rules: no attachments (link instead), no charts in the body (link to dashboards), no FYI items (those go in the self-service pointer).
Test readability: have someone scan the template in 30 seconds and tell you what is on track and what is blocked. If they cannot, simplify.

steps.description: After the first month, check whether the updates are being read and whether they are changing decisions. If not, the system needs revision.

outputs.name: readership-data
outputs.desc: Who opens the updates, who acts on them, who ignores them

outputs.name: revision-plan
outputs.desc: Specific changes to cadence, content, or audience based on the feedback

process: After 4 weeks, check open rates (if email) or ask directly: are you reading these? What do you use from them?
If a stakeholder is not reading, either they do not need the update (remove them) or the update does not contain what they need (fix the content).
If the update is read but not producing decisions, the content is informational, not actionable. Add a decision prompt: 'Action needed: approve X by Friday.'
Revise and re-test. The system is working when every reader can name a decision the update influenced.

description: Deliver feedback using the SBIR model: Situation, Behavior, Impact, Request. Track whether feedback produces change. If the same feedback is delivered three times with no change, the problem is structural, not behavioral.

steps.description: Isolate the specific situation where the behavior occurred. Feedback without a specific situation becomes a character judgment. 'In last Tuesday's client call' not 'generally speaking.'

inputs.name: behavior-to-address
inputs.desc: What behavior you need to give feedback on

inputs.name: recipient-context
inputs.desc: Your relationship to the person and the context in which you work together

outputs.name: situation-anchor
outputs.desc: The specific date, time, meeting, conversation, or event where the behavior occurred

outputs.name: pattern-or-one-off
outputs.desc: Whether this is a single instance or a pattern, and the evidence for each

process: Name the exact situation: date, event, participants. 'In the Tuesday 3pm product review with the engineering team.'
Determine if this is a pattern or a one-off. A pattern requires at least 3 instances. Two is a coincidence, not a pattern.
If it is a pattern, list the instances. If it is a one-off, acknowledge that in your delivery. 'I noticed something in Tuesday's meeting' lands differently than 'You always do this.'
Feedback on a pattern is harder to deliver but more important. Feedback on a one-off should be lighter in weight.

steps.description: Describe the behavior using only what was observable. No interpretation of intent, no adjectives, no generalizations. Behavior is what a camera would record.

inputs.name: situation-anchor
inputs.desc: When and where the behavior happened

outputs.name: behavior-description
outputs.desc: The observable behavior, free of interpretation

outputs.name: intent-assumptions-removed
outputs.desc: Interpretations you removed from the description (saved so you can check yourself)

process: Write what the person did using verbs, not adjectives. 'Interrupted the presenter twice during slides 3 and 7' not 'was rude.'
Remove every attribution of intent. You do not know their intent. You know their behavior.
Remove every generalization. 'You interrupted twice' not 'you always interrupt.'
Test: could the person agree that this is what happened, even if they disagree about whether it was a problem? If yes, the description is clean.

steps.description: Connect the behavior to its impact. Impact is what makes feedback useful instead of annoying. Without impact, feedback is 'I noticed a thing.' With impact, feedback is 'this thing caused a problem.'

inputs.name: recipient-context
inputs.desc: The person's role and what they care about

outputs.name: impact-statement
outputs.desc: The specific consequence of the behavior on the work, the team, the relationship, or the outcome

outputs.name: impact-evidence
outputs.desc: Observable evidence of the impact (not your feeling about it, but the measurable result)

process: Name the impact: 'The presenter lost her place and the client asked to move on, so we did not cover the pricing section.'
Connect impact to something the recipient cares about. If they care about client relationships, lead with the client impact.
Use 'I' language for emotional impact: 'I felt the meeting went off track' not 'You derailed the meeting.'
Keep impact to 1-2 sentences. Impact that takes a paragraph to explain is probably multiple feedback items. Separate them.

steps.description: Make a specific, actionable request for change. 'Be more respectful' is not actionable. 'Let the presenter finish each slide before asking questions' is actionable.

inputs.name: pattern-or-one-off
inputs.desc: Whether this is a pattern, which affects the weight of the request

outputs.name: change-request
outputs.desc: The specific behavior change you are requesting

outputs.name: success-measure
outputs.desc: How both of you will know the change has happened

process: State the behavior you want to see instead. Positive framing: 'Hold questions until the end of each section' not 'Stop interrupting.'
Make it measurable: both of you should be able to observe whether the change happened.
For a pattern, the request is stronger: 'I need this to change starting now.' For a one-off, lighter: 'Can you try X next time?'
One request per feedback session. Multiple requests dilute each other and feel like an attack.

steps.description: Track whether feedback produces change. Set a follow-up date, observe the behavior, and close the loop. If the same feedback is delivered three times with no change, escalate from behavioral feedback to structural change (process, role, environment).

inputs.name: success-measure
inputs.desc: How you will know it changed

outputs.name: follow-up-plan
outputs.desc: When to check, what to observe, and what to do if change happened or did not happen

outputs.name: structural-escalation-criteria
outputs.desc: The threshold (3 instances of same feedback) at which you stop giving behavioral feedback and change the structure

process: Set a follow-up observation window: 2 weeks for behavioral changes, 1 month for habit changes.
During the window, observe the behavior against the success measure. Do not give more feedback during the window. Give the person time.
At follow-up: if the behavior changed, acknowledge it explicitly. Recognition of change reinforces change.
If the behavior did not change after 3 feedback cycles, the problem is not behavioral. Change the process, the role, the environment, or the team composition.

description: Map stakeholders on influence and interest to design communication strategy for each group. Most communication failures happen when you treat a high-influence stakeholder like a low-interest one. Works for any project, proposal, or initiative with multiple people who can affect the outcome.

steps.description: List every person who can affect or is affected by the outcome. Include the ones who are not in the room but could block the result from outside it.

inputs.name: initiative-description
inputs.desc: The project, proposal, or initiative you are mapping stakeholders for

inputs.name: known-stakeholders
inputs.desc: The people you already know are involved

outputs.name: full-roster
outputs.desc: Every person who can affect the outcome, including hidden influencers and potential blockers

outputs.name: hidden-stakeholder-notes
outputs.desc: People not in the obvious list who could affect the outcome from outside the project

process: List every person in the formal approval chain: who signs off, who funds, who manages the team doing the work.
List every person affected by the outcome: whose workflow changes, whose budget is impacted, whose team is restructured.
List hidden stakeholders: the executive's trusted advisor, the long-tenured employee whose opinion carries informal weight, the customer who will be vocal.
For each person, write one sentence about their relationship to the initiative. If you cannot, you do not know enough about them yet.

steps.description: Score each stakeholder on two dimensions: influence (their power to affect the outcome) and interest (how much they care). Use evidence, not assumptions.

outputs.name: scored-roster
outputs.desc: Each stakeholder with influence score (1-5) and interest score (1-5) with evidence for each

outputs.name: quadrant-assignment
outputs.desc: Each stakeholder assigned to a quadrant: Manage Closely, Keep Satisfied, Keep Informed, Monitor

process: Score influence from 1 (no power to affect outcome) to 5 (can approve, veto, or kill the initiative). Evidence: their role, their budget authority, their political capital.
Score interest from 1 (does not know or care about the initiative) to 5 (deeply invested in the outcome, checks on it regularly). Evidence: their questions, their meeting attendance, their emails.

Assign quadrants: high influence + high interest = Manage Closely. High influence + low interest = Keep Satisfied. Low influence + high interest = Keep Informed. Low influence + low interest = Monitor.
Flag mismatches: a high-influence stakeholder you have been treating as low-interest is your biggest risk.

steps.description: Design a communication strategy for each quadrant. The strategy for a high-influence, high-interest stakeholder (1-on-1 meetings, early previews, input on decisions) is different from a low-influence, high-interest one (regular updates, feedback opportunities).

outputs.name: communication-plan-per-quadrant
outputs.desc: For each quadrant: frequency, format, content, and owner of the communication

outputs.name: individual-plans
outputs.desc: For Manage Closely stakeholders, an individual communication plan for each person

process: Manage Closely (high influence, high interest): 1-on-1 meetings, early previews before group announcements, input on key decisions, direct access to the project lead.
Keep Satisfied (high influence, low interest): brief periodic updates on outcomes (not details), early warning on anything that might concern them, minimal time asks.
Keep Informed (low influence, high interest): regular group updates, feedback opportunities, recognition of their input even when it cannot change the direction.
Monitor (low influence, low interest): general announcements only. Do not spend time on custom communication for this group.

steps.description: Stakeholder influence and interest shift over time. A quarterly review catches shifts before they cause a communication failure.

outputs.name: review-schedule
outputs.desc: When and how to review the map (quarterly or at major milestones)

outputs.name: shift-indicators
outputs.desc: Signals that a stakeholder's influence or interest has changed (new questions, missed meetings, new budget authority, org changes)

process: Set a quarterly review cadence tied to project milestones or organizational changes.
At each review, re-score each stakeholder. Has their authority changed? Have they started or stopped paying attention?

Define shift indicators: a stakeholder who starts asking detailed questions has moved from low-interest to high-interest. A stakeholder who stops attending meetings has moved from high-interest to low-interest.
When a stakeholder changes quadrants, update their communication plan immediately. The lag between quadrant shift and communication update is where failures happen.

description: Build a revision system for written communication. First draft: write everything. Second pass: cut what does not advance the reader toward action. Third pass: replace abstract words with concrete ones. Fourth pass: conclusion first. The test: can the reader act after the first paragraph?

steps.description: Define what the reader should do after reading. If you do not know, you are not ready to write. Every sentence that does not move the reader toward that action is a sentence to cut.

inputs.name: draft-or-topic
inputs.desc: The message, email, memo, or proposal you are writing or revising

inputs.name: reader-description
inputs.desc: Who will read this and what role they play

outputs.name: reader-action
outputs.desc: The specific action the reader should take after reading, in one sentence

outputs.name: reader-questions
outputs.desc: The questions the reader needs answered before they can take that action

process: Write the action in one sentence: 'Approve the budget by Friday.' 'Schedule a meeting with the vendor.' 'Stop doing X and start doing Y.'
If the piece is informational (no action required), state the takeaway: 'Understand that X changed and what it means for their work.'
List the questions the reader will have before acting: How much does it cost? What is the timeline? What happens if they say no?
Your message must answer these questions. Anything else is decoration.

steps.description: Write the first draft without editing. Get everything out. The first draft is for the writer. Every subsequent draft is for the reader.

inputs.name: reader-questions
inputs.desc: The questions the reader needs answered

outputs.name: raw-draft
outputs.desc: The complete first draft, unedited

outputs.name: word-count
outputs.desc: The word count of the first draft, which will be the high-water mark

process: Write everything you know about the topic. Do not stop to edit, restructure, or polish.
Include context, background, reasoning, evidence, caveats, and the ask. It will be too long. That is correct for a first draft.
Record the word count. Your final draft should be 30-50% of this number.

steps.description: Second pass: for each sentence, ask 'does this move the reader toward the action?' If not, cut it. The most common mistake in written communication is including context the writer needed but the reader does not.

inputs.name: reader-action
inputs.desc: The action the reader should take

outputs.name: trimmed-draft
outputs.desc: The draft with non-action-advancing sentences removed

outputs.name: cut-log
outputs.desc: Sentences removed and why, in case any need to be restored

process: Read each sentence. Ask: if I remove this sentence, can the reader still take the action? If yes, cut it.
Watch for throat-clearing: 'As you know,' 'It is worth noting that,' 'For context,' These phrases almost always precede cuttable content.
Watch for writer-therapy: paragraphs that explain how you arrived at the recommendation. The reader does not care about your process. They care about the conclusion.
Move cut sentences to a log. Some belong in the appendix or a supporting document, not in the trash.

steps.description: Third pass: replace every abstract word with a concrete one. 'Significant cost savings' becomes '$340K annually.' 'Soon' becomes 'by March 15.' Abstract words let the reader fill in their own meaning, which is usually wrong.

inputs.name: trimmed-draft
inputs.desc: The draft after cutting non-essential sentences

outputs.name: concrete-draft
outputs.desc: The draft with abstract words replaced by specific, measurable language

outputs.name: abstraction-log
outputs.desc: Abstract words replaced and their concrete replacements

process: Search for abstract quantity words: 'significant,' 'substantial,' 'many,' 'some,' 'various,' 'several.' Replace with numbers.
Search for abstract time words: 'soon,' 'shortly,' 'in the near future,' 'eventually.' Replace with dates.
Search for abstract quality words: 'improved,' 'better,' 'enhanced,' 'streamlined.' Replace with what specifically changed and by how much.
Test: could two readers disagree about what a sentence means? If yes, it contains an abstraction. Make it specific.

steps.description: Fourth pass: put the conclusion first. The reader should be able to act after the first paragraph. Everything after the first paragraph is supporting evidence for readers who need it.

outputs.name: final-draft
outputs.desc: The restructured message with conclusion first, evidence second, background last

outputs.name: one-paragraph-test-result
outputs.desc: Whether the first paragraph alone is sufficient for the reader to act

process: Move the conclusion and the ask to the first paragraph. 'I recommend we do X by Y date because Z.'
Follow with the evidence that supports the conclusion, ordered by strength.
Place background and context last. Most readers will not need it. Those who do will find it at the end.
Test: read only the first paragraph. Can you act? If yes, the structure is correct. If no, the first paragraph is missing the ask or a key fact.

steps.description: Final check: read the piece aloud. If you stumble on a sentence, the reader will stumble too. If a sentence needs to be read twice, rewrite it.

outputs.name: published-message
outputs.desc: The final, checked message ready to send

outputs.name: word-count-reduction
outputs.desc: Percentage reduction from first draft to final draft

process: Read the piece aloud. Mark every sentence where you stumble, pause, or need to re-read.
Rewrite marked sentences. If a sentence is longer than 25 words, split it. If it has more than one comma, simplify.
Check the word count against the first draft. A good revision cuts 30-50%. If you cut less than 20%, you were not ruthless enough.
Send it.

description: Design meetings that produce decisions, not discussions. Circulate the decision (not a topic) and pre-read before the meeting. Discuss only disagreements. End with a decision, owners, and deadlines. If no decision can be made, end the meeting and define what is needed to decide.

steps.description: Frame the meeting around a decision, not a topic. 'Should we hire a contractor or build in-house?' not 'Let's discuss the project staffing.' A meeting without a decision to make is an email.

inputs.name: meeting-purpose
inputs.desc: Why you think a meeting is needed

inputs.name: attendee-list
inputs.desc: Who needs to be in the room and why

outputs.name: decision-statement
outputs.desc: The specific decision to be made, phrased as a question with a finite set of answers

outputs.name: options-list
outputs.desc: The options on the table, each with a one-line description of trade-offs

outputs.name: meeting-necessity-check
outputs.desc: Whether this meeting is actually needed or could be replaced by async communication

process: State the decision as a question: 'Should we [option A] or [option B]?' with at most 3-4 options.
For each option, write the trade-off in one sentence: what you gain and what you lose.
Check necessity: if one person can make this decision with async input, cancel the meeting and send the decision in writing.
A meeting is necessary only when the decision requires real-time discussion because the trade-offs are ambiguous or politically sensitive.

steps.description: Build the pre-read: the document attendees must read before the meeting. The pre-read contains the decision, the options, the data, and the recommendation. The meeting is for disagreements, not summaries.

outputs.name: pre-read-document
outputs.desc: The document containing decision, options, data, and recommendation, under 2 pages

outputs.name: distribution-plan
outputs.desc: When to send the pre-read (at least 24 hours before the meeting) and to whom

process: Write the pre-read: page 1 is the decision and options. Page 2 is the supporting data and your recommendation.
The recommendation section says what you would do and why. Attendees who agree do not need to speak in the meeting.
Send the pre-read at least 24 hours before the meeting. Tag it clearly: 'Pre-read required for [meeting name].'
If the pre-read is longer than 2 pages, it contains material that belongs in an appendix, not the pre-read.

steps.description: Open the meeting by checking whether everyone read the pre-read. If they did not, cancel the meeting and reschedule. Meetings where half the room has not read the pre-read produce discussions, not decisions.

outputs.name: readiness-check-result
outputs.desc: Whether the meeting proceeds or is rescheduled

outputs.name: meeting-rules
outputs.desc: The rules for the meeting: discuss disagreements only, time-boxed, decision at the end

process: Spend the first 2 minutes asking: 'Has everyone read the pre-read?' If more than one person has not, reschedule.
If everyone has read it, state the rules: 'We are here to decide [decision]. The recommendation is [X]. We will discuss only where you disagree with the recommendation.'
Set the time box: 'We have [N] minutes. We will decide by the end or define what we need to decide next time.'
Do not summarize the pre-read. That rewards the people who did not read it.

steps.description: Facilitate the discussion by focusing only on disagreements with the recommendation. Agreement does not need airtime. Silence is agreement.

outputs.name: disagreement-log
outputs.desc: Each disagreement stated, the person who raised it, and whether it was resolved in the meeting

outputs.name: new-information
outputs.desc: Any new information surfaced during discussion that changes the trade-offs

process: Ask: 'Who disagrees with the recommendation, and why?' Go around the room or ask for hands.
For each disagreement, clarify: is this new information that changes the trade-offs, or a difference in values or priorities?
New information is resolved with data. Value differences are resolved by the decision-maker weighing the trade-offs.
If a disagreement cannot be resolved in the meeting, note what would resolve it (data, analysis, external input) and assign an owner.

steps.description: Close the meeting with the decision, the owners, and the deadlines. Read them aloud. If anyone is confused about what was decided, clarify now. Ambiguity at this stage multiplies into wasted work.

inputs.name: disagreement-log
inputs.desc: What disagreements were raised and resolved

outputs.name: decision-record
outputs.desc: What was decided, by whom, with what caveats

outputs.name: action-items
outputs.desc: Each action, its owner, and its deadline

outputs.name: next-meeting-criteria
outputs.desc: If no decision was made: what is needed to decide and when to reconvene

process: State the decision aloud: 'We decided to [option]. [Person] owns implementation. Deadline is [date].'
For each action item: name the owner and the deadline. Do not assign actions to groups. Assign to one person.

If no decision was made: state what information is needed, who will get it, and when the group reconvenes. Do not schedule another meeting to 'continue the discussion.' Schedule a meeting to make the decision with the missing information.
Send the decision record within 1 hour of the meeting ending. Delay allows memory to edit what was actually decided.
